name: Siwa Oasis: an island of Berbers in the Egyptian desert
note: Orientation: 560 km from Cairo, 50 km from Libya, below sea level, 300,000 date palms, 70,000 olive trees, salt lakes, springs; Amazigh (Berber) Siwi speakers, 'Isiwan'; isolated until the 1980s road; conservative customs; what to see in a day.

name: Marsa Matruh and the road to Siwa
note: Ancient Paraetonium where Alexander turned inland toward Siwa in 331 BC; Cleopatra's Beach and the legend of her bathing with Antony; Rommel's Cave museum and the 1942 campaign; then 300 km south through nothing: the Qattara Depression to the east, the escarpment, first palms.

name: Rommel, Montgomery and the desert war around here
note: Short. Rommel's HQ cave at Matruh, El Alamein 1942 just east, Siwa used by the Long Range Desert Group and briefly by Italians; minefields still in parts of the desert, which is why guides keep to tracks.

name: The Great Sand Sea
note: 72,000 km2 of dunes between Egypt and Libya, some over 100 m, ridges running N-S for 100+ km; Gerhard Rohlfs 1874 named it; sea fossils (shells, sea urchins) on the floor from the Tethys; Libyan desert glass; safety: 4x4 convoys, GPS, the old Darb routes.

name: Bir Wahed: hot and cold springs in the dunes
note: Short. A hot sulphur spring and a cold lake 15 km into the dunes, drilled by oil prospectors; sunset tea with the camp; the stars (no light pollution); what to bring.

name: Libyan desert glass: the meteorite in Tutankhamun's pectoral
note: Yellow-green natural glass strewn over the Great Sand Sea 150 km SE of Siwa, formed ~29 million years ago by a meteorite impact/airburst; the central scarab of Tutankhamun's pectoral (GEM) is carved from it; Clayton's 1932 find; why you should not pick it up (export ban).

name: The lost army of Cambyses
note: Herodotus: 50,000 Persians sent by Cambyses II in 524 BC to destroy the Oracle of Amun, swallowed by a sandstorm; claimed discoveries (Castiglioni brothers 2009, bones and bronze); the sceptics (Olaf Kaper: Petubastis III revolt cover story); why Siwans like the tale.

name: Temple of the Oracle of Amun at Aghurmi
note: 26th Dynasty (Amasis, c. 550 BC) temple on the Aghurmi rock inside a mud-brick village; one of the great oracles of the ancient Mediterranean alongside Delphi; Croesus and Lysander consulted it; the hidden side corridor where priests may have spoken; Alexander's visit 331 BC; the view from the rock over the palms.

name: Alexander the Great at the Oracle, 331 BC
commons: Alexander the Great Siwa oracle Ammon coin horns
note: The trek from Paraetonium guided by ravens/snakes, rain in the desert; the priest's greeting 'son of Zeus-Ammon' (or a mispronounced 'o paidion'); what he asked; the ram's horns on his coins; the persistent legend that he is buried in Siwa (Souvaltzi 1995 claim, rejected); Greek-Egyptian link for a Greek visitor.

name: Temple of Umm Ubayda (Amun's second temple)
note: 30th Dynasty temple of Nectanebo II a few hundred metres from Aghurmi, linked by a processional way; blown up in 1896 by an Ottoman governor for building stone, one inscribed wall left standing with reliefs of Amun; the procession of the oracle's barque between the two temples.

name: Gebel al-Mawta, the Mountain of the Dead
note: Conical hill honeycombed with rock-cut tombs from the 26th Dynasty to Roman times; Siwans sheltered in them from Italian bombing in 1940 and looted paintings; the four painted tombs; what you see: Greek-Egyptian mixed style; sunset view.

name: Tomb of Si-Amun
note: Finest tomb: a wealthy Greek-Egyptian (curly hair, beard, Greek-style) shown with Egyptian gods; Nut on the ceiling, Osiris, Thoth; 3rd century BC; the damage from 1940 and from tourists' flash; the family scene.

name: Tombs of Mesu-Isis, Niperpathot and the Crocodile
note: Niperpathot: oldest (26th Dynasty), red-ink inscriptions, 'prophet of Osiris'; Mesu-Isis: cobras frieze over the entrance; Crocodile tomb: a yellow crocodile (Sobek) painted, Ptolemaic. Short per tomb.

name: Shali Fortress: the melted mud city
note: Founded 1203 by seven families after attacks; built of kershef (salt-rock + mud + palm) up to five storeys inside one gate (later two, three); nobody lived outside until 1826; three days of rain in 1926 melted it and the town moved out; partially restored since 2018 (EU/Environmental Quality International); climb it at sunset; the old mosque with its minaret.

name: Cleopatra's Spring (Ain Guba, Spring of Juba)
note: Round stone pool fed by a natural spring on the road to Aghurmi; Herodotus' 'Fountain of the Sun' (cool by day, warm at night) is probably this or nearby; Cleopatra never came (the name is tourist-era); Juba may be Juba II of Mauretania who wrote on Libya; bathing etiquette (women cover up).

name: Dakrur Mountain: sand baths and the Siyaha festival
note: Twin-humped hill where Siwans bury rheumatism patients in hot sand in July-August; the three-day Siyaha (Eid el-Siyaha) festival of reconciliation each October full moon, all men eat together on the mountain (dates may coincide with the visit: October full moon 2026 is around the 26th); the view.

name: Fatnas Island: sunset over the salt lake
note: Short. Palm-covered islet in Birket Siwa reached by a causeway; the sunset tea ritual; Birket Siwa is salt water from a dying lake, the oasis' drainage problem (rising groundwater from unmanaged springs).

name: Siwa's salt lakes and the floating pools
note: Turquoise salt pools (around Zeitoun/the Ras Zeitoun salt works) where you float like the Dead Sea; salt crust, salt mining and export, salt lamps and salt bricks; Birket Siwa and Birket Zeitoun as the oasis' drainage; don't get the water in your eyes.

name: Siwi people, the Siwa House and the market
note: Amazigh language Siwi (unwritten, ~20,000 speakers); the House of Siwa Museum (built 1990 by a Canadian ambassador to save the architecture); wedding silver and the 'adrim' disc, embroidered dresses, pottery; the famous dates (saidi, frehi) and olive oil; women rarely seen in public, covered in blue-grey tarfottet; the 'zaggalah' bachelor workers legend; market etiquette.

name: The Qattara Depression and why Siwa is below sea level
note: Short. Siwa sits 19 m below sea level; Qattara to the east reaches -133 m; the never-built plan to flood it from the Mediterranean for hydro power; why springs flow (artesian Nubian sandstone aquifer); the salt marsh (sabkha) you see on the road.
